title_en: Peng Lijing v. Liang Xiping, Wang Baoshan, and Hebei Golden Coast Real Estate Development Co., Ltd. — dispute over infringement of equity transfer
ruling_gist_en: 1. Where both spouses jointly contribute capital to establish a company, they should use their respective property as registered capital and each bear corresponding liabilities. Therefore, when registering the company, the spouses should submit a property division certificate. If no property division is made, it should be deemed that the spouses contributed capital using their jointly owned property to establish the company. During the existence of the marital relationship, the company shares registered in either spouse's name belong to the jointly owned property of the spouses. As joint co-owners, the spouses enjoy equal rights of possession, use, benefit, and disposal over such property.

full_text_en:
Peng Lijing v. Liang Xiping, Wang Baoshan,

Hebei Golden Coast Real Estate Development Co., Ltd.

— Dispute over Infringement of Equity Transfer

【Ruling Summary】

I. Where a husband and wife jointly contribute capital to establish a company, they shall use their respective owned property as registered capital and bear corresponding liabilities respectively. Therefore, when registering a company, the husband and wife shall submit a property division certificate. If no property division is made, the husband and wife shall be deemed to have made capital contributions to the company with their jointly owned property. During the existence of the marital relationship, the company shares held in the name of the husband or wife shall constitute property jointly owned by both spouses. As joint co-owners, the husband and wife have equal rights to possess, use, benefit from, and dispose of such property.

II. Pursuant to paragraph 2 of Article 17 of the Interpretation (I) of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of the Marriage Law of the People's Republic of China, where a husband or wife makes an important decision concerning jointly owned property not arising from daily living needs, the husband and wife shall consult each other on an equal footing and reach a consensus. If others have reason to believe that the disposition made by one spouse represents the common intent of both spouses, the other spouse may not assert the defense of disagreement or lack of knowledge against a bona fide third party. Therefore, the act of one spouse transferring jointly owned company shares constitutes an important disposition of jointly owned property, which shall require the consensus of both spouses and their joint signatures on the equity transfer agreement, the shareholders' resolution, and the amendment to the articles of association.

III. Where shares of a company are jointly owned by both spouses, the validity of an equity transfer agreement entered into by one spouse with a third party shall be comprehensively analyzed based on the facts of the case, in conjunction with factors such as whether the other spouse had actual knowledge of the equity transfer and whether the transferee acted in good faith. If it can be determined that the other spouse had knowledge of the equity transfer and the transferee acted in good faith, the equity transfer agreement shall be binding on the other spouse.

Civil Judgment of the Supreme People's Court

(2007) Min Er Zhong Zi No. 219

Appellant (Plaintiff at First Instance): Peng Lijing, female, Han ethnicity, born November 24, 1975, residing at Room 1-403, No. 56 Xinhua West Road, Xinhua District, Shijiazhuang City, Hebei Province.

Agent ad litem: Shi Jianzhong, lawyer of Beijing Xinhe Law Firm.

Appellee (Defendant at First Instance): Liang Xiping, male, Han ethnicity, born April 24, 1971, residing at Room 2-302, Building 58, Bolin Residential Area, Xinhua District, Shijiazhuang City, Hebei Province.

Agent ad litem: Gao Yang, lawyer of Hebei Jiangzhong Law Firm.

Appellee (Defendant at First Instance): Wang Baoshan, male, Han ethnicity, born June 28, 1955, residing at Room 5-303, Dormitory of the Provincial Economic Cooperation Office, Qiaoxi District, Shijiazhuang City, Hebei Province.

Agent ad litem: Gao Xiuping, lawyer of Hebei Xinye Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Fan Yunping, lawyer of Hebei Zhengda Xiangshi Law Firm.

Appellee (Defendant at First Instance): Hebei Golden Coast Real Estate Development Co., Ltd., domiciled at 12th Floor, Xiqing Apartment, No. 25 Hongqi Street, Shijiazhuang City.

Legal Representative: Wang Baoshan, Executive Director of the Company.

Agent ad litem: Liu Shibin, lawyer of Beijing Shuangli Law Firm.

Appellant Peng Lijing, in the case of dispute over infringement of equity transfer against Appellees Liang Xiping, Wang Baoshan, and Hebei Golden Coast Real Estate Development Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Golden Coast Company), appealed against the Civil Judgment (2007) Ji Min Er Chu Zi No. 18 of the Hebei High People's Court to this Court. This Court formed a collegial panel with Trial Judge Jin Jianfeng serving as the Presiding Judge, Trial Judge Wang Dongmin, and Adjudicating Judge Yin Yuan participating in the trial, with Court Clerk Zhao Suijun taking records. The case has now been concluded.

The facts found by the court of first instance: On November 7, 2005, the plaintiff Peng Lijing and the defendant Liang Xiping, as Party A, entered into a contract with the defendants Wang Baoshan and Wang Junshi as Party B, reaching an agreement on the transfer of equity in Golden Coast Company and related matters. The contents included: 1. Company's business project status: 1.1. Golden Coast Company was established on January 27, 2005, with a registered capital of RMB 8,000,000. Liang Xiping and Peng Lijing contributed RMB 6,400,000 and RMB 1,600,000 respectively, holding 80% and 20% respectively. 1.2. On February 5, 2005, Hebei Army Reserve Infantry Division (hereinafter referred to as the Reserve Division) transferred its land in the Gaozhuang camp area through a competitive bidding sale of land有偿转让, and Golden Coast Company won the bid; on March 8 of the same year, Golden Coast Company entered into a "Military Land Transfer Contract" with the Reserve Division; on March 8 of the same year, the General Logistics Department of the People's Liberation Army, through its Reply No. (2005) Hou Ying Zi No. 568 "Regarding the Transfer of Part of the Land by the Hebei Army Reserve Infantry Division," approved the Reserve Division to transfer to Golden Coast Company 277,014.3 square meters of land (demolishing 38,232 square meters of buildings) located at Gaozhuang Village, Huolu Town, Luquan City, Hebei Province, on three plots with military land certificates Jing Ji Zi No. 2819, 2766, and 2767. The transfer procedures were currently in process. Golden Coast Company had already paid a total of RMB 8,640,300 in land transfer fees and deposits to the "Land Administration Bureau of the General Logistics Department of the People's Liberation Army," "Joint Logistics Department of the Beijing Military Region," and the "Reserve Division," and still needed to pay an additional RMB 20,432,400 in land transfer fees, as well as handle residual issues such as evicting lessees (occupants). 2. Equity value and equity shares: 2.1. Party A, Liang Xiping and Peng Lijing, had invested significant manpower and financial resources in obtaining the project. After negotiation and agreement between Party A and Party B, the equity value of the former shareholders of Golden Coast Company, Liang Xiping and Peng Lijing, was determined to be RMB 61,200,000 (including the land transfer fees and deposits of RMB 8,640,300 previously paid to the military and the RMB 20,432,400 still to be paid to the Reserve Division), and this equity value was to be transferred to Party B, Wang Baoshan and Wang Junshi. 2.2. Of the total equity value of RMB 61,200,000, Liang Xiping held 80% shares, with an equity value of RMB 48,960,000, and Peng Lijing held 20% shares, with an equity value of RMB 12,240,000. 3. Equity transfer: 3.1. Within 20 days after the contract was signed, Party A's Liang Xiping and Party B's Wang Baoshan would begin the procedures for the 80% equity transfer (Wang Baoshan would not pay the equity transfer price temporarily, but would pay in accordance with the terms set out in Article 7.1), and Party A would assist Party B's Wang Baoshan in carrying out the change of business registration of Golden Coast Company, with costs to be borne by Party B's Wang Baoshan. After the change, the legal representative of Golden Coast Company would be Wang Baoshan. At the same time, Party A's Liang Xiping would deliver to Party B's Wang Baoshan all accounts, statements, seals, bid-winning notices, and other relevant documents of Golden Coast Company according to the handover list agreed upon by both parties. 3.2. When Party B paid the last installment of the debt referred to in Article 7.1 of this contract, Party A's Peng Lijing and Party B's Wang Junshi would carry out the 20% equity transfer procedures of Golden Coast Company. Party A's Peng Lijing would assist Party B's Wang Junshi in carrying out the change of business registration of Golden Coast Company, with costs to be borne by Party B's Wang Junshi. 3.3. After this contract is signed, both parties shall strictly perform it. If there is a breach, the breaching party shall, in addition to compensating the non-breaching party for direct losses, pay a penalty of RMB 2,000,000. 4. Payment of remaining land transfer fees: 4.1. Within 20 days after the contract is signed, Party B shall pay, on behalf of Golden Coast Company, RMB 15,000,000 in land transfer fees to the Reserve Division (including the RMB 2,000,000 already paid into the designated account of the Reserve Division). This contract shall take effect from the date of such payment. The remaining RMB 5,432,400 shall be negotiated directly by Party B's Wang Baoshan, on behalf of Golden Coast Company, with the Reserve Division. 4.2. If the "Military Land Transfer Contract" cannot be performed due to issues with the payment of the remaining land transfer fees, Party B shall pay Party A liquidated damages of RMB 30,000,000, with Yalong Company and Longji Company assuming joint and several guarantee liability. 5. Establishment of debt for unpaid equity transfer price: The equity values of Party A's Liang Xiping and Peng Lijing were converted into RMB 61,200,000. Party A's Liang Xiping transferred his 80% equity in Golden Coast Company to Party B's Wang Baoshan, with the transfer price converted into RMB 48,960,000 (including the RMB 20,432,400 land transfer fees payable to the Reserve Division), and the remaining balance of RMB 29,007,600 was to be paid by Wang Baoshan to Party A's Liang Xiping in the form of debt within the time limit set forth in Article 7.1 of this contract; Party A's Peng Lijing transferred her 20% equity in Golden Coast Company to Party B's Wang Junshi, with the transfer price converted into RMB 12,240,000, to be paid by Wang Junshi to Party A's Peng Lijing in the form of debt within the time limit set forth in Article 7.1 of this contract. 6. Other expenses: The clearance costs of RMB 1,885,000 incurred by Golden Coast Company in the process of clearing lessees (occupants) on the land of this project shall be borne by the post-change Golden Coast Company, with any excess to be resolved by negotiation between Party A and Party B. 7. Handling of claims and debts: 7.1. Within 10 days after the land use right certificate is changed to the name of the post-change Golden Coast Company, Party B's Wang Baoshan shall pay RMB 10,000,000 in debt to Party A's Liang Xiping; the remaining RMB 30,767,600 (including the RMB 12,240,000 owed to Party A's Peng Lijing) shall be paid by Party B in installments of RMB 10,000,000 every three months after the first payment of RMB 10,000,000, with the final installment of RMB 10,767,600 to be settled by December 30, 2006. 13. This contract shall take effect after being signed by all four persons of Party A and Party B and Golden Coast Company, and the guarantee contract shall take effect after being sealed by each guarantor. Liang Xiping, Wang Baoshan, Golden Coast Company, Shijiazhuang Yuanda Municipal Engineering Co., Ltd., Yalong Company, and Longji Company signed and sealed. Peng Lijing and Wang Junshi did not sign the contract. During the trial, the plaintiff acknowledged the authenticity of this evidence but did not accept the content of the contract, arguing that the subject of the contract was unqualified, the expression of intent was untrue, defendant Liang Xiping did not have the inherent authority to represent the plaintiff Peng Lijing, and defendant Wang Baoshan did not have written evidence proving the plaintiff Peng Lijing's participation in the equity transfer process.

On November 8, 2005, Golden Coast Company held a shareholders' meeting and passed a resolution to change shareholders and transfer capital contributions, resolving that original shareholder Liang Xiping would transfer his 80% equity to the new shareholder Wang Baoshan, and other shareholders waived their preemptive rights. The resolution bore the signatures and fingerprints of Liang Xiping, Peng Lijing, and Wang Baoshan. During the trial investigation, all parties had no objection to the authenticity of this evidence. The plaintiff Peng Lijing did not acknowledge her signature and fingerprint, claiming they were forged by Wang Baoshan and Liang Xiping. Defendant Liang Xiping admitted that the plaintiff Peng Lijing's signature and fingerprint were signed and affixed by him on her behalf.

On November 23, 2005, Peng Lijing, Liang Xiping, and Wang Baoshan passed an amendment to the articles of association of Golden Coast Company, amending the company's domicile from No. 261 Jianshe North Street, Shijiazhuang City, to No. 25 Hongqi Street, Shijiazhuang City; and amending the names of the company's shareholders from Liang Xiping and Peng Lijing to Wang Baoshan and Peng Lijing. The amendment bore the signatures and fingerprints of Liang Xiping, Peng Lijing, and Wang Baoshan. During the trial investigation, all parties had no objection to the authenticity of this evidence. The plaintiff Peng Lijing did not acknowledge her signature and fingerprint, claiming they were forged by Wang Baoshan and Liang Xiping. Defendant Liang Xiping admitted that the plaintiff Peng Lijing's signature and fingerprint on the amendment were signed and affixed by him on her behalf.

After the equity transfer contract was signed, on November 23, 2005, the parties changed the company's business registration, changing the original shareholder Liang Xiping to Wang Baoshan, holding 80% of the company's equity, with the plaintiff Peng Lijing still holding 20% of the company's equity. Wang Baoshan successively paid a total of RMB 49,440,000 in equity transfer price to the couple Liang Xiping and Peng Lijing. Among these, on behalf of Golden Coast Company, on September 28, September 29, and December 1, 2005, a total of RMB 20,432,400 in land transfer fees was paid to the Reserve Division in three installments, and RMB 29,007,600 in equity transfer price (including a RMB 100,000 loan made to the plaintiff Peng Lijing on September 30, 2005) was paid to the couple Liang Xiping and Peng Lijing, totaling RMB 49,440,000. During the trial, the plaintiff Peng Lijing had no objection to the authenticity of the payment receipts, but argued that among all written evidence of the performance of the equity transfer contract, except for the receipt for the loan of RMB 100,000 on September 30, 2005, which bore her signature, there was no other signature of the plaintiff. Defendant Wang Baoshan had no evidence that the plaintiff Peng Lijing had received the equity transfer price, so the equity transfer price was irrelevant to this case. The plaintiff only borrowed RMB 100,000, but the loan receipt was not an equity transfer contract and was unrelated to the equity transfer price. Defendant Liang Xiping had no objection to the authenticity of the equity transfer price of RMB 49,440,000 and the payment receipts. However, he argued that the flow of funds was entirely controlled by himself and had nothing to do with others. He also admitted that the plaintiff Peng Lijing initially participated in the negotiation of the equity transfer, but negotiations were suspended due to differences. The final equity transfer contract was signed without the plaintiff Peng Lijing's knowledge, and the performance of the contract and the flow of payments were all handled by him alone.

On November 9, 2005, the plaintiff Peng Lijing and the defendant Liang Xiping newly registered and established Hebei Coast Real Estate Development Co., Ltd. at the former domicile of Golden Coast Company, with a registered capital of RMB 8,000,000. Peng Lijing held 20% of the company's shares, Liang Xiping held 80%, and Peng Lijing served as the executive director and was the legal representative of the company.

To prove that the plaintiff Peng Lijing had knowledge of the equity transfer, the defendant Wang Baoshan provided two witnesses to the court: the intermediary Yin Guangzong and Longji Company's accountant Qie Rongna. Among them, the intermediary Yin Guangzong was the deputy director of the Administrative Project Management Center of the Shijiazhuang Development and Reform Commission. Defendant Liang Xiping was introduced to defendant Wang Baoshan through him, and he participated in the entire process of the equity transfer of Golden Coast Company. Witness Qie Rongna was the financial officer of Longji Company and participated in the preliminary payment and the financial handover of Golden Coast Company. During the trial, witness Yin Guangzong testified: "The participants included Liang and Peng and their lawyer, and Wang and his lawyer. The drafting of the contract was done by a lawyer surnamed Zhao. Both parties were satisfied, and under this framework, both parties further negotiated and revised, and then finalized the contract. The parties signed the contract in Wang Baoshan's office. After signing, Wang Baoshan asked to see the original military approval documents, because during the negotiations Liang Xiping only brought copies, so Peng Lijing took us to the military to see the originals. After seeing the originals, the parties continued to perform the contract as agreed, going through the transfer procedures. Wang Baoshan paid the first payment of RMB 100,000, the second payment of RMB 2,000,000, and the subsequent payments I don't know. One year after completion, Peng Lijing and Liang Xiping came to me again. Peng Lijing asked for an additional 10 mu of land for housing based on the original contract. Both sides were unhappy about this. Peng Lijing and Liang Xiping came to my office together, and I tried to mediate, asking both sides to make concessions. But later the lawsuit happened, and I don't know the details." Witness Qie Rongna testified: "On September 28, 2005, I accompanied Liang Xiping to the Qiaodong Sub-branch to deliver a check of RMB 1,000,000 to the military, and on September 29, I went to the bank to deliver another check of RMB 1,000,000 to the military. These RMB 2,000,000 were remitted from Yalong Company and Longji Company respectively. The legal representatives of both companies at that time were Wang Baoshan. I asked Liang Xiping for a receipt, and he told me to ask the military for a receipt. When I went to the military, they were on holiday, so the receipt was issued together when the second payment was made later. Later, on December 1, when the second payment was made, I had the receipt for the original amount supplemented, and I had it issued in two separate receipts. On September 30, Mr. Wang told me to take RMB 100,000 to his office. At that time, Peng Lijing and Liang Xiping were both present. Peng Lijing took the RMB 100,000 and wrote an IOU. On January 14, 2006, I and two other colleagues of the company went to Golden Coast Company to hand over financial accounts. There were issues with the accounts. The accountant of Golden Coast Company called to consult someone, addressing the other party as 'General Peng,' and the cashier also said that without Peng Lijing's consent, they could not issue the counterfoil."

Regarding the testimony of the two witnesses, the plaintiff Peng Lijing argued that witness Yin Guangzong initially claimed that he had "poor memory and could not remember clearly," and almost every sentence contained vague words like "it seems," so Yin Guangzong was unqualified as a witness. Witness Qie Rongna was a financial employee of the company in which Wang Baoshan was a shareholder and chairman, and had an interest in the defendant Wang Baoshan. Therefore, the testimony of the two witnesses could not be used as evidence. Defendant Liang Xiping argued that the testimony of witness Yin Guangzong was inconsistent with the statement of defendant Wang Baoshan and should not be accepted. The testimony of witness Qie Rongna was uncorroborated and should not be accepted by the court either.

Peng Lijing filed the lawsuit on March 23, 2007, requesting: 1. To confirm that the provisions in the equity transfer contract and its appendices signed by defendant Liang Xiping and Wang Baoshan, regarding the transfer of the plaintiff's 20% equity in Golden Coast Company to others at a price of RMB 12,240,000, violated the plaintiff's lawful rights and interests and are not binding on the plaintiff. 2. To confirm that the provisions in the equity transfer contract and its appendices signed by defendant Liang Xiping and Wang Baoshan, regarding the transfer of defendant Liang Xiping's 80% equity in Golden Coast Company to defendant Wang Baoshan at a price of RMB 48,960,000, violated the plaintiff's lawful rights and interests such as the preemptive right, and are void. And to order the three defendants to take necessary measures such as handling the change of company registration, to transfer the 80% equity in Golden Coast Company that defendant Wang Baoshan acquired from defendant Liang Xiping to the plaintiff, to ensure that the plaintiff realizes her preemptive right in accordance with the law, and to ensure that the plaintiff's equity value is not harmed. 3. To have the three defendants bear all litigation costs.

The court of first instance held that the key issues in dispute were: 1. Whether Golden Coast Company had legal personality. 2. As a shareholder of Golden Coast Company, whether defendant Liang Xiping had the authority to act on behalf of the plaintiff Peng Lijing in entering into the equity transfer contract, the shareholders' resolution, and the amendment to the articles of association, and whether the equity transfer contract was binding on the plaintiff Peng Lijing. 3. The validity of the equity transfer contract.

Regarding the Determination of Jinhai'an Company's Corporate Personality. Through the court hearing, it is known that the defendant Liang Xiping and the plaintiff Peng Lijing are husband and wife. The couple invested a portion of their jointly owned property as their respective capital contributions in a limited liability company and registered the establishment of Jinhai'an Company. In this regard, the defendant Wang Baoshan argues that Peng Lijing and Liang Xiping, as a married couple, did not partition their jointly owned property. Although the registered shareholders are two persons, they are in essence a collective whole, and the relationship between the husband and wife does not constitute a genuine shareholder relationship under the Company Law. He contends that the corporate personality of Jinhai'an Company should be disregarded. It must be clarified that China's Company Law imposes no restriction on the identity of shareholders. The joint investment by a husband and wife in establishing a limited liability company does not violate any prohibitive provisions of the law. Furthermore, Article 23 of the Several Provisions on Certain Issues concerning Company Registration Administration, promulgated by the State Administration for Industry and Commerce, provides that "where family members jointly invest to establish a limited liability company, they must use their respective owned property as registered capital and bear corresponding liabilities respectively, and a written certificate or agreement on property partition must be submitted at the time of registration." Therefore, a husband and wife may jointly invest to establish a limited liability company. In fact, using undivided jointly owned marital property as capital contribution to establish a company does not necessarily impair the independence of the company's property. It merely meets the requirements for establishing the company and satisfies the registration authority's demands. The investment proportions shown in the industrial and commercial registration do not alter or partition the jointly owned marital property, nor can they be simplistically equated to a property agreement between the spouses. Accordingly, Peng Lijing and Liang Xiping's use of undivided jointly owned marital property as capital contribution to establish Jinhai'an Company complies with the Company Law, and Jinhai'an Company possesses an independent corporate personality. The defendant Wang Baoshan's assertion cannot be sustained, and this court does not adopt it.

Regarding the Issue of Whether the Defendant Liang Xiping Had the Authority to Represent the Plaintiff Peng Lijing. Since the plaintiff Peng Lijing and the defendant Liang Xiping both deny the existence of any authorization, and there is no other direct evidence proving an agency relationship between them. However, the special feature of this case is that the plaintiff Peng Lijing and the defendant Liang Xiping are husband and wife, and Jinhai'an Company was established by them as a couple. This special and specific identity relationship results in the internal governance of Jinhai'an Company differing from that of an ordinary limited liability company. The relationship between Liang Xiping and Peng Lijing is very close in the eyes of a third party, concerning both family and personal matters. Yet it is insufficient to conclude that the defendant Liang Xiping necessarily possesses agency authority solely based on this special relationship, especially when dealing with non-routine matters. Paragraph 2 of Article 17 of the Interpretation (I) of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues concerning the Application of the Marriage Law of the People's Republic of China provides: "Where a husband or wife makes an important decision on jointly owned property not due to daily living needs, the husband and wife shall consult each other on an equal footing and reach a consensus. If another person has reason to believe that such a decision represents the common intention of both spouses, the other spouse may not oppose a bona fide third party on the ground of disagreement or lack of knowledge." From the foregoing, the key issue is whether the defendant Wang Baoshan had reason to believe that this disposition of jointly owned family property represented the common intention of both spouses, and whether Wang Baoshan acted in good faith—that is, whether he, as the counterparty, knew at that time that Liang Xiping's act constituted unauthorized agency.

The court of first instance held that the defendant Liang Xiping had the authority to represent the plaintiff Peng Lijing in signing the shareholders' meeting resolution, the amendment to the company's articles of association, and the equity transfer contract, and had the authority to dispose of the 20% equity interest in Jinhai'an Company held by Peng Lijing. The reasons are as follows:

1. The plaintiff Peng Lijing and the defendant Liang Xiping, as a married couple, met the defendant Wang Baoshan through the intermediary Yin Guangzong in order to pay the land transfer fee to the reserve division. Under the facilitation of the intermediary Yin Guangzong, both parties began negotiating the equity transfer. This fact indicates that the plaintiff Peng Lijing was not unaware of the equity transfer; on the contrary, she actively participated in the negotiation, and the transfer of equity was the true common intention of the couple.

2. Before signing the agreement, the defendant Wang Baoshan had already paid RMB 2 million of the land transfer fee to the reserve division in the name of Jinhai'an Company, demonstrating his sincerity in acquiring the equity through concrete actions. After the defendant Liang Xiping signed the equity transfer agreement with the defendant Wang Baoshan, he received the subsequent equity transfer payments. Given the pre-existing circumstance that the couple had jointly negotiated and agreed to transfer the equity to the defendant Wang Baoshan, it was sufficient to lead one to believe that Liang Xiping's act of disposing of all the company's equity was a manifestation of the common intention of Peng Lijing and Liang Xiping as a couple, and was an act by Liang Xiping representing both spouses in disposing of jointly owned property, rather than an act by Liang Xiping alone without authorization. It should be noted that the defendant Wang Baoshan had no other business dealings with Jinhai'an Company. Wang Baoshan was introduced to the defendant Liang Xiping by the intermediary Yin Guangzong, and Wang Baoshan's payment of the equity transfer price to Liang Xiping was in performance of the equity transfer contract, and nothing else.

3. The plaintiff Peng Lijing, from the initiation of the lawsuit to the present, has not submitted any evidence to the court proving that the defendant Wang Baoshan acted in bad faith during the equity transfer process. She merely claims that she was unaware of the equity transfer and did not sign the equity transfer contract. During the court hearing, the defendant Liang Xiping stated that during the negotiations, the plaintiff Peng Lijing once suspended the equity transfer negotiations due to a difference of opinion, and that he then transferred the equity without her knowledge, but he did not adduce evidence to support this claim. The defendant Wang Baoshan denied the statements made by the couple. On the contrary, the witness Yin Guangzong, provided by the defendant Wang Baoshan, testified in court that after the equity transfer contract was signed, the plaintiff Peng Lijing brought the defendant Wang Baoshan and him to the reserve division to verify the originals of the relevant documents for the transferred land, and that one year after the contract was performed, Peng Lijing and Liang Xiping came to his office and asked him to persuade Wang Baoshan to allocate an additional 10 mu of land for them to build their own house. Although the plaintiff Peng Lijing and the defendant Liang Xiping denied the testimony of the witness Yin Guangzong, and although the witness Yin Guangzong repeatedly stated during his testimony that "a long time has passed, I might not remember clearly" and "it's not my own business," it cannot be denied that, as an intermediary, Yin Guangzong's testimony was objective and truthful. That is, the plaintiff Peng Lijing was aware of the equity transfer, and the couple's intention to transfer Jinhai'an Company was consistent and genuine. The series of evidence provided by the defendant Wang Baoshan proves that he had reason to believe that the defendant Liang Xiping had the authority to represent the plaintiff Peng Lijing in signing the equity transfer contract. The plaintiff Peng Lijing's denial of the equity transfer on the ground of lack of knowledge defies common sense. The defendant Liang Xiping only stated in court that the plaintiff Peng Lijing had interrupted the negotiations midway and that the equity would no longer be transferred, but he could not adduce any evidence that he had notified the defendant Wang Baoshan and the intermediary Yin Guangzong to suspend the negotiations. Therefore, the statements of the plaintiff Peng Lijing and the defendant Liang Xiping cannot be sustained.

4. The plaintiff Peng Lijing argues that Wang Baoshan failed to exercise the duty of care and should have sought ratification after the equity transfer contract was signed. However, after the lawsuit was filed, both the plaintiff Peng Lijing and the defendant Liang Xiping respectively wrote to the defendant Wang Baoshan, urging him to complete the land transfer procedures. In particular, the plaintiff Peng Lijing referred to the defendant Wang Baoshan as "the controlling shareholder of Jinhai'an Company." This fact shows that the plaintiff Peng Lijing was not only aware of the equity transfer in Jinhai'an Company but also subsequently ratified the act of Liang Xiping signing on her behalf, thereby confirming the equity transfer contract.

5. Clause 4.1 of the equity transfer contract stipulates: "Within 20 days after the signing of this contract, Party B (Wang Baoshan) shall, in the name of Jinhai'an Company, pay the land transfer fee of RMB 15 million to the reserve division (including the RMB 2 million previously deposited into the designated account of the reserve division). This contract shall take effect from the date of Party B's payment of this amount." This clause provides the same conditions for the plaintiff Peng Lijing, who claims a right of first refusal. However, under the then-existing circumstances, the plaintiff Peng Lijing did not have the ability to pay this amount. Therefore, her claim of a right of first refusal cannot be sustained.

Based on the foregoing facts and reasons, although the defendant Liang Xiping's act of transferring the equity of Jinhai'an Company had procedural defects—namely, the lack of the plaintiff Peng Lijing's signature—it does not bind the defendant Wang Baoshan, who acted as a bona fide third party. Liang Xiping's disposal constitutes apparent authority, and it is presumed that he had the right to sign the shareholders' meeting resolution, the amendment to the company's articles of association, and the equity transfer contract on behalf of the plaintiff Peng Lijing, thereby disposing of the company's equity. The plaintiff Peng Lijing's claim that the defendant Wang Baoshan infringed upon her right of first refusal and her right to object cannot be sustained, and this court does not adopt it.

Even assuming, arguendo, that the defendant Liang Xiping did not have the authority to represent the plaintiff Peng Lijing in signing the equity transfer contract, the shareholders' meeting resolution, and the amendment to the company's articles of association to transfer the equity, the defendant Wang Baoshan has adduced evidence proving that he is a bona fide third party, with sufficient reason to believe that the defendant Liang Xiping had agency authority. Moreover, the defendant Wang Baoshan has paid the defendant Liang Xiping RMB 49.44 million in equity transfer consideration, a valuable consideration, and has completed the procedures for changing the shareholders of Jinhai'an Company. Article 89 of the Opinions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues concerning the Implementation of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China (for Trial Implementation) provides: "Where, during the continuance of a joint ownership relationship, one of the joint owners disposes of the jointly owned property without authorization, such disposition shall generally be deemed invalid. However, if a third party acquires the property in good faith and for value, the lawful rights and interests of the third party shall be protected, and any loss incurred by other joint owners shall be compensated by the person who disposed of the jointly owned property without authorization." That is, even if Liang Xiping had no right to dispose of the jointly owned property, from the perspective of fairness and to protect transaction security, the lawful rights and interests of the defendant Wang Baoshan should be protected. As for the losses caused to Peng Lijing by Liang Xiping's act, she may separately seek compensation from the defendant Liang Xiping. Moreover, Jinhai'an Company was registered by Peng Lijing and Liang Xiping with their jointly owned property. The couple's ownership of the joint property is not proportional co-ownership, nor is it separate ownership; it is joint ownership. According to the law, as joint owners, the husband and wife enjoy equal rights to possess, use, dispose of, and benefit from the jointly owned property. The equity transfer funds that the defendant Liang Xiping has received from the defendant Wang Baoshan for Jinhai'an Company fall within the scope of the jointly owned property of Liang Xiping and Peng Lijing. Therefore, the plaintiff Peng Lijing's claim cannot be sustained, and this court does not adopt it.

Regarding the Validity of the Equity Transfer Contract. Clause 13 of the equity transfer contract stipulates: "This contract shall become effective upon being signed by both parties (four individuals) and Jinhai'an Company; the guarantee contract shall become effective upon being sealed by each guarantor." The plaintiff Peng Lijing relies on this provision to argue that the contract has not satisfied the agreed effective conditions and the statutory requirements for validity, and thus should not be protected by law. However, in reality, the equity transfer contract contains two effective clauses. In addition to the above clause, Clause 4.1 of the contract also stipulates: "Within 20 days after the signing of this contract, Party B (Wang Baoshan) shall, in the name of Jinhai'an Company, pay the land transfer fee of RMB 15 million to the reserve division (including the RMB 2 million previously deposited into the designated account of the reserve division). This contract shall take effect from the date of Party B's payment of this amount." Between these two clauses, Clause 4.1 constitutes a substantive conditional effective clause for the entire contract, i.e., within 20 days after the contract is signed, the defendant Wang Baoshan must pay the land transfer fee of RMB 15 million to the reserve division in the name of Jinhai'an Company. Once Wang Baoshan pays this amount, the equity transfer contract takes effect. In fact, the defendant Wang Baoshan did pay the land transfer fee to the reserve division within 20 days after signing the contract, thereby satisfying the effective condition stipulated in the contract. Moreover, before the contract was signed, the defendant Wang Baoshan had already paid RMB 2 million of the land transfer fee to the reserve division in the name of Jinhai'an Company, thereby substantially performing the main obligations under the contract. The plaintiff Peng Lijing and the defendant Liang Xiping were aware of this and accepted it without any objection. Pursuant to Article 37 of the Contract Law, where a contract is to be concluded in written form, if one party has performed the main obligations prior to signing or sealing, and the other party has accepted the performance, the contract is concluded. Clause 13 of the equity transfer contract, in relation to the entire contract, is merely a formality requirement. Indeed, Peng Lijing and Wang Junshi did not sign the contract, so there is a formal defect. However, Liang Xiping signed the contract, and the defendant Wang Baoshan has performed the main contractual obligations and acted in good faith. Furthermore, the defendant Liang Xiping, as the husband of the plaintiff Peng Lijing, had the right to sign the equity transfer contract, the shareholders' meeting resolution, and the amendment to the company's articles of association on behalf of the plaintiff Peng Lijing. Therefore, the contract took effect and has been performed. As for the plaintiff Peng Lijing's claim that the content of the equity transfer contract is illegal, on the ground that the defendants Liang Xiping and Wang Baoshan colluded maliciously, infringing upon her right of first refusal and her statutory right to transfer equity, and that the contract is void: during the court hearing, the plaintiff Peng Lijing did not provide any evidence proving malicious collusion between the defendants Wang Baoshan and Liang Xiping. Additionally, for the reasons stated above, Liang Xiping's act does not constitute an infringement and constitutes apparent authority. Therefore, the equity transfer contract represents the true intention of both parties, its content does not violate laws or regulations, and it is valid. The plaintiff Peng Lijing's claim lacks factual and legal basis, and this court does not support it.

The plaintiff Peng Lijing's lawsuit is an equity transfer dispute. The subject of the equity transfer is the shareholders of Jinhai'an Company, not the company itself. Moreover, during the equity transfer process, Jinhai'an Company did not commit any infringement against the plaintiff Peng Lijing, nor does the plaintiff Peng Lijing have any evidence proving that Jinhai'an Company had any fault in the equity transfer process. Therefore, this claim by the plaintiff Peng Lijing is entirely without factual or legal basis, and this court does not support it.

The court of first instance, pursuant to Articles 128 and 138 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, Article 37 and Paragraph 1 of Article 45 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China, Paragraph 2 of Article 17 of the Interpretation (I) of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues concerning the Application of the Marriage Law of the People's Republic of China, and Article 89 of the Opinions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues concerning the Implementation of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China (for Trial Implementation), rendered the following judgment: the plaintiff Peng Lijing's claims are dismissed; the case acceptance fee of RMB 316,010 and the preservation fee of RMB 5,000 shall be borne by the plaintiff Peng Lijing.

Peng Lijing, dissatisfied with the above civil judgment of the court of first instance, appealed to this court, arguing: 1. The court of first instance violated Articles 79 and 64 of the Several Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Evidence in Civil Proceedings. The judgment of first instance neither specified which evidence was admitted nor explained the reasons for admitting or not admitting evidence. To prove that the appellant Peng Lijing was aware of the equity transfer, the appellee Wang Baoshan presented two witnesses to the court. The statement of the intermediary Yin Guangzong was either not corroborated by other evidence or conflicted with other evidence. The witness Qie Rongna is a financial staff member of the company in which Wang Baoshan is a shareholder and chairman of the board, and has an interest relationship with Wang Baoshan. The judgment of first instance admitted the testimony without providing any reasons. 2. The facts found in the judgment of first instance are either not supported by any valid evidence or are completely contrary to the facts that valid evidence can prove. On November 7, 2005, the plaintiff Peng Lijing and the defendant Liang Xiping, as Party A, signed a contract with the defendants Wang Baoshan and Wang Junshi, as Party B, regarding the transfer of equity in Jinhai'an Company and related matters. Only Liang Xiping and Wang Baoshan signed this contract; Peng Lijing and Wang Junshi did not sign. The first instance found that before the contract was signed, Wang Baoshan had already paid RMB 2 million of the land transfer fee to the reserve division in the name of Jinhai'an Company, thereby substantially performing the main obligations under the contract. Wang Baoshan successively paid RMB 49.44 million in equity transfer consideration to Liang Xiping and his wife, but Peng Lijing never knew about the payment of equity transfer consideration or the amount. 3. The court of first instance erred in the application of law. (1) A key issue in this case is whether Wang Baoshan is a bona fide third party. He should bear the burden of proving that he had reason to believe that the transfer of equity was the common intention of both Peng Lijing and Liang Xiping. The court of first instance reversed the burden of proof onto Peng Lijing without legal basis. (2) After filing the lawsuit, Peng Lijing wrote to the defendant Wang Baoshan, urging him to complete the land transfer procedures. In the letter, Peng Lijing referred to the defendant Wang Baoshan as "the controlling shareholder of Jinhai'an Company." The court of first instance relied on this letter to conclude that Peng Lijing was not only aware of the equity transfer in Jinhai'an Company but also subsequently ratified Liang Xiping's act of signing on her behalf, confirming the equity transfer contract. The court of first instance's reliance on this letter was unfounded. (3) The court of first instance ignored the fact that neither Peng Lijing nor Wang Junshi signed the contract, and that Peng Lijing's equity was infringed upon, and reached the conclusion that "Peng Lijing did not have the ability to pay this amount under the circumstances at that time, so her claim of a right of first refusal cannot be sustained," which has no factual or legal basis. (4) Regarding the validity of the equity transfer contract, the judgment of first instance held that both Clause 13 and Clause 4.1 of the equity transfer contract stipulated conditions for the contract to take effect. Since the contract contains two clauses concerning its effectiveness, according to the principles of company law, equity transfer must be effected by a written contract. Based on the principles of contract and contract law, the signing or sealing by the parties is a necessary element for the formation of a contract, and the validity of a contract presupposes its formation. Therefore, even if Clause 4.1 constitutes a substantive conditional effective clause for the entire contract, it still requires the formation of the contract as a prerequisite. In other words, if the equity transfer contract at issue has not yet satisfied the effective formation conditions stipulated in Clause 13, how can it be said to take effect under Clause 4.1? Thus, the court of first instance's determination that the contract became effective upon Wang Baoshan's payment under Clause 4.1, while disregarding Clause 13, contravenes the fundamental principles of the Contract Law. In summary, the court of first instance committed serious violations in the review and admission of evidence and the reasoning thereof, in the determination of facts, and in the application of law. Peng Lijing requests that the judgment of first instance be set aside and that a new judgment be rendered based on the facts ascertained.

Appellee Liang Xiping responded in his defense: 1. The signature and fingerprint of Peng Lijing on the "Equity Transfer Agreement" were indeed not made by Peng Lijing herself but were jointly forged by the respondent and Wang Baoshan. At the time of signing, Liang Xiping, Wang Baoshan, and Yin Guangzong were present. Peng Lijing and Wang Junshi were not present, and Peng Lijing had no knowledge of the contents of this agreement. 2. The signature of Peng Lijing on the "Shareholders' Resolution" was also forged. At that time, it was at Wang Baoshan's place, and Peng Lijing was not present. Liang Xiping signed and affixed fingerprint in the presence of Wang Baoshan and Yin Guangzong. The signature and fingerprint were not Peng Lijing's, and all three knew this. 3. The industrial and commercial registration was primarily handled by Yin Guangzong. The signatures and fingerprints on a series of documents were forged as discussed by the three, and Wang Baoshan was well aware of this. 4. Peng Lijing initially participated in the negotiations, but later she disagreed with the transfer and withdrew. She also disagreed with Liang Xiping continuing to discuss the transfer with Wang Baoshan. Liang Xiping verbally agreed but actually handled the transfer matters together with Wang Baoshan. Peng Lijing had no knowledge of the entire process. 5. Before the equity transfer, Peng Lijing borrowed RMB 100,000 from Wang Baoshan. The signature of Peng Lijing on that document was genuine. This RMB 100,000 was unrelated to the equity transfer and was a personal loan. The signature of Peng Lijing on the IOU was completely different from the signature on the agreement, which Wang Baoshan knew. 6. During the period when the three privately handled the equity transfer, Peng Lijing was resting at home due to pregnancy and did not participate in the management of any company. She had no knowledge of the payment of the transfer price. By the time she learned of it, the matter was already concluded. She became very angry after learning and later filed the lawsuit. 7. Yin Guangzong participated in the entire process of forging signatures on the transfer agreement, shareholders' resolution, and industrial and commercial change registration documents. Yin Guangzong was also the general manager hired by Wang Baoshan's company, and his testimony was false and untrue. In summary, the respondent indeed wronged Peng Lijing. She had no knowledge of the equity transfer process, and the forged signatures were primarily done on the advice of Wang Baoshan. Neither Liang Xiping nor Wang Baoshan was a bona fide third party, and the respondent requests a fair judgment from the court.

Appellee Wang Baoshan responded in his defense: 1. The court of first instance examined and determined all evidence submitted by Peng Lijing and Wang Baoshan in accordance with the requirements of the Supreme People's Court's Several Provisions on Evidence in Civil Proceedings. In this case, issues such as whether the "Contract" for the equity transfer of Golden Coast Company was legally binding on Peng Lijing could not be determined based on a single piece of evidence. A correct judgment could only be made by comprehensively considering the five pieces of evidence submitted by Peng Lijing, the twenty-two pieces of evidence submitted by Wang Baoshan, and the statements of Liang Xiping and Golden Coast Company. The judgment of first instance, based on the statements of the parties and the evidence submitted and after cross-examination, comprehensively examined and judged the different forms of evidence. The determination on whether evidence was admitted and the reasons therefor were clearly stated in the "Facts Found" and "Opinion of the Court" sections. Therefore, Peng Lijing's claim that the "judgment of first instance did not clarify which evidence was admitted, nor did it explain the reasons for admitting or not admitting evidence" is untenable. 2. The judgment of first instance found the fact that "Peng Lijing and Wang Junshi did not sign the contract." Based on the five pieces of evidence provided by Peng Lijing, the twenty-two pieces of evidence provided by Wang Baoshan, and the statement of Liang Xiping, it concluded: "The equity transfer contract represents the true intention of both parties, its content does not violate laws or regulations, and it is a valid agreement." The judgment of first instance found that before the conclusion of the "Contract," Peng Lijing knew that Wang Baoshan had already paid RMB 2 million in land transfer fees to the Reserve Division in the name of Golden Coast Company without raising any objection, and that Wang Baoshan had actually performed the principal obligations under the contract. Peng Lijing knew that Wang Baoshan had paid RMB 49.44 million in transfer price to the couple Peng Lijing and Liang Xiping. The two other companies jointly owned by the couple Peng Lijing and Liang Xiping, Yuanda Company and Coast Company, received subsequent equity transfer payments of RMB 28,907,600 from Wang Baoshan. Since Yuanda Company and Coast Company received such a huge amount of equity transfer fees from Wang Baoshan, Peng Lijing should have known the fact of the equity transfer. 3. Regarding the application of law by the court of first instance. On Peng Lijing's claim that Wang Baoshan should bear the burden of proof on whether he was bona fide: Wang Baoshan provided twenty-two pieces of evidence within the time limit for evidence submission set by the court of first instance, and these formed a complete evidentiary chain, sufficient to prove that Wang Baoshan was a bona fide third party in this equity transfer process. According to the principle of "he who asserts must prove," if Peng Lijing claims that Wang Baoshan acted in bad faith, she should provide evidence to prove Wang Baoshan's bad faith. However, to date, Peng Lijing has not provided any evidence that Wang Baoshan acted in bad faith when acquiring the equity in Golden Coast Company. On Peng Lijing's right of preemption: All equity in Golden Coast Company was jointly owned by the couple Peng Lijing and Liang Xiping. This was a fact admitted by both the appellant Peng Lijing and the respondent Wang Baoshan. According to the provisions of China's civil law, during the subsistence of a co-ownership relationship, a joint co-owner does not enjoy the right to divide or transfer, the right to claim partition, or the right of preemption. Peng Lijing's claim that she enjoyed a right of preemption when her husband Liang Xiping transferred the equity in Golden Coast Company, which was jointly owned by the couple, has no basis. On the issue of Liang Xiping's authority of agency: The judgment of first instance, while assuming that Liang Xiping had no authority to sign the equity transfer contract, shareholders' resolution, and amendment to the company's articles of association on behalf of Peng Lijing, held that Wang Baoshan had proven his good faith and had reason to believe that Liang Xiping had authority to act, thus concluding that Wang Baoshan's legitimate rights and interests should be protected. On the formation and entry into effect of the "Equity Transfer Contract": The judgment of first instance, based on the fact that Wang Baoshan had performed the principal obligations under the "Contract," determined pursuant to Article 37 of the Contract Law that even though Peng Lijing did not sign the "Contract," the "Contract" had been validly formed; and based on the fact that Wang Baoshan had fulfilled the condition for entry into effect stipulated in Article 4.1 of the "Contract" — "paying RMB 15 million in land transfer fees to the Reserve Infantry Division in the name of Golden Coast Company" — correctly determined that the "Contract" had entered into effect.

Appellee Golden Coast Company responded in its defense: 1. Peng Lijing's naming of the respondent as a defendant in this case has no factual or legal basis. The judgment of first instance correctly dismissed Peng Lijing's claim against the respondent. Peng Lijing's lawsuit is a dispute over infringement of equity transfer rights. In this case, the transferors are the couple Peng Lijing and Liang Xiping, and the transferees are Wang Baoshan and Wang Junshi, not the respondent. The respondent's act of conducting the equity change registration in accordance with the law, based on legal documents such as the equity transfer agreement signed by the parties, did not infringe any rights of Peng Lijing and was not at fault. Therefore, Peng Lijing's tort lawsuit against the respondent is completely without legal basis, and the judgment of first instance correctly dismissed her claim. 2. The transfer of all equity in Golden Coast Company by the couple Peng Lijing and Liang Xiping to Wang Baoshan represented the true intention of both parties. The transfer was lawful and valid and should be protected by law. The judgment of first instance correctly confirmed that the "Equity Transfer Contract" dated November 7, 2005, was lawful, valid, and legally binding on Peng Lijing. 3. Peng Lijing's application for the court of first instance to seal the respondent's land has no basis and has already caused significant economic losses to the respondent's development and operations. The court of second instance should lift the seal as soon as possible. The respondent will also pursue legal remedies for the losses caused by Peng Lijing. 4. The respondent agrees with all defense arguments of Wang Baoshan.

This Court, upon trial, confirms the facts found by the court of first instance.

Opinion of the Court: The content and form of the equity transfer contract in this case do not violate the mandatory provisions of laws or regulations. The equity transfer has been actually performed, and the company change registration has been completed. Therefore, it should be determined that the equity transfer contract is lawful and valid. The appellant Peng Lijing claims that since she did not sign the equity transfer contract, the contract is void. Article 13 of the "Equity Transfer Contract" in this case stipulates: This contract shall become effective upon signature by all four parties, A and B, and Golden Coast Company, and the guarantee contracts shall become effective upon affixing the seals of each guarantor. The appellant Peng Lijing claims that the contract did not satisfy the agreed conditions for entry into effect and the statutory requirements for valid formation and thus should not be protected by law. However, the equity transfer contract stipulates two entry-into-effect clauses. In addition to the above clause, Article 4.1 of the contract also stipulates: "Within 20 days after the signing of the contract, Party B (Wang Baoshan) shall pay the land transfer fee of RMB 15 million to the Reserve Division in the name of Golden Coast Company (including the RMB 2 million previously transferred to the account designated by the Reserve Division). The contract shall become effective upon the payment of this sum by Party B." Between these two clauses, the stipulation in Article 4.1 of the contract is a conditional entry-into-effect clause. Wang Baoshan actually performed the contract. The condition for the entry into effect of the equity transfer contract was satisfied, and the contract was validly formed. Therefore, the equity transfer contract became effective and was actually performed. The fact that Peng Lijing did not sign the "Equity Transfer Contract" is merely a defect in the procedure for the shareholder to handle the share transfer and company change. This defect did not affect the actual performance of the equity transfer contract. Peng Lijing knew of this and did not object. Therefore, the defect in the equity transfer does not affect the validity of the equity transfer contract.

Regarding the validity of Liang Xiping signing the equity transfer contract, shareholders' resolution, and amendment to the company's articles of association on behalf of Peng Lijing: The appellant Peng Lijing and the appellee Liang Xiping are husband and wife. Golden Coast Company was solely established by the couple. The husband, Liang Xiping, held 80% of the shares, and the wife, Peng Lijing, held 20% of the shares. When a couple contributes capital to establish a company, they should each use their own property as registered capital and bear corresponding responsibilities individually. Therefore, the couple should have submitted a property division certificate when registering the company. However, in this case, the couple did not divide their property when establishing the company, and it should be held that the company was established with capital contributed from their jointly owned marital property. Peng Lijing and Liang Xiping used their jointly owned marital property to contribute capital to establish the company. During the subsistence of their marital relationship, the company shares of the husband or wife constitute jointly owned property of the couple. As joint co-owners, the couple enjoys equal rights to possess, use, benefit from, and dispose of the jointly owned property. According to Article 17, paragraph 2 of this Court's Interpretation (I) of Several Issues Concerning the Application of the Marriage Law of the PRC: "If a husband or wife makes an important decision regarding the jointly owned marital property not for daily living needs, the husband and wife shall negotiate on an equal footing and reach a consensus. If others have reason to believe that it is the common intention of both husband and wife, the other party may not resist a bona fide third party on the grounds of disagreement or lack of knowledge." The act of Peng Lijing and Liang Xiping transferring the equity of Golden Coast Company constituted an important decision regarding jointly owned marital property. Both of them should have signed the equity transfer contract, shareholders' resolution, and amendment to the company's articles of association. However, regarding the validity of Liang Xiping signing the contract and signature on behalf of Peng Lijing, it should be comprehensively analyzed and determined based on the facts of this case, taking into account whether Peng Lijing knew of the equity transfer and whether Wang Baoshan was bona fide. The facts found in this case are as follows: Peng Lijing and Liang Xiping were introduced to Wang Baoshan by the intermediary Yin Guangzong and jointly negotiated the equity transfer matters. Before signing the equity transfer agreement, Wang Baoshan paid RMB 2 million in land concession fees to the Reserve Division in the name of Golden Coast Company using the military unit's account provided by the appellant couple. When signing the equity transfer agreement, the Shijiazhuang Yuanda Municipal Engineering Co., Ltd., jointly established by the couple, provided a guarantee. After signing the equity transfer agreement, Wang Baoshan delivered the equity transfer payments to Yuanda Company and Hebei Coast Real Estate Development Co., Ltd., which were jointly established by the couple. Wang Baoshan held a copy of Peng Lijing's identity card and handled the industrial and commercial registration for the equity change. Wang Baoshan held all the original licenses, seals, and documents of Golden Coast Company, and the registered address of Golden Coast Company was changed. Wang Baoshan had paid RMB 49.44 million in equity transfer payments, completed the shareholder formalities for Golden Coast Company, and after the performance of the equity transfer contract, actually controlled Golden Coast Company. The above facts prove that the appellant Peng Lijing participated in the signing and performance of the equity transfer, and the transfer of equity was the true intention of the couple. Wang Baoshan had reason to believe that Liang Xiping could represent his wife Peng Lijing in signing the equity transfer contract, shareholders' resolution, and amendment to the company's articles of association. Liang Xiping stated that Peng Lijing had stopped negotiations midway and that the equity would no longer be transferred. However, Peng Lijing could not provide evidence proving whether she notified Wang Baoshan of the termination of the equity transfer. Peng Lijing knew the fact of the equity transfer but did not raise any objection or prevent her husband Liang Xiping from transferring her shares. This should be deemed as consent to the transfer. Liang Xiping's signing and signature on the equity transfer contract on behalf of Peng Lijing is binding on Peng Lijing. Peng Lijing argued on appeal that the parties to the equity transfer contract, Liang Xiping and Wang Baoshan, engaged in malicious collusion, infringing upon her right of preemption. However, Peng Lijing did not provide any evidence proving the facts of malicious collusion between Wang Baoshan and Liang Xiping constituting infringement. Therefore, the appellant Peng Lijing's request to confirm the transfer contract as void on the grounds that she did not sign the equity transfer contract or the shareholders' resolution, and her claim that the appellees Liang Xiping and Wang Baoshan engaged in malicious collusion infringing her right of preemption, lack factual and legal basis. Her grounds for appeal are untenable, and this Court does not support them.

In summary, the court of first instance had clear factual findings, sufficient evidence, and correctly applied the law. Peng Lijing's contentions and grounds on appeal have no factual basis or legal support, and her appeal is not sustained. Pursuant to Article 153, paragraph 1, subparagraph (1) of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC, the judgment is as follows:

Appeal dismissed and the original judgment affirmed.

The appellate court acceptance fee in the amount of RMB 316,010 shall be borne by Peng Lijing.

This judgment is final.
